quizzes.title: 18.1 Module 18 Introduction: Asia in Arms
quizzes.description:
MODULE INTRODUCTION
Module Introduction: Asia in Arms
Survey · 2 questions · not graded
≈ ─ ≈ ─ ≈
Before you start

Welcome to Asia in Arms. Answer the questions below before you open the first lesson. Your answers help your teacher see where the class is starting. This survey is not graded.

This module's goals:
  • Describe how the Nationalists and the Communists rose, fought, and survived in China.
  • Explain how militarism and the Mukden Incident put Japan’s army in command.
  • Weigh whether Japan’s road to war was chosen or forced.

questions.text: Before you read: Was Japan’s road to war chosen or forced? Give your first answer in two or three sentences. You will answer it again at the end of the module, so it is fine if your answer changes.
I have read this module's goals and I know what I am working toward this week.

answers.text: Yes, I have read them
Not yet, I will read them before the first lesson

quizzes.title: 18.7 Reading Quiz: Asia in Arms
quizzes.description:
READING QUIZ
Reading Quiz: Asia in Arms
7 questions · 7 points
≈ ─ ≈ ─ ≈
Before you start

This quiz covers both lessons and both primary sources for this module. It has 7 questions. Most ask you to work something out from what you read, not to find a sentence in the text. You may look back at the lessons and sources while you work.

HOW TO WORK
Read the two lessons and the two primary sources first, and keep your notes in My Notebook. Then answer the questions below.

questions.text: After the killings of 1927, why was Mao’s turn to the countryside a sensible choice for the Communists who survived?

answers.text: Soviet advisers had ordered it, and Moscow’s orders were always followed
Nine in ten Chinese lived in the countryside, Chiang held the cities, and the peasants had gained little under his rule
The warlords had promised to protect any Communist who reached their villages
Japan had offered land to every peasant who would join the Red Army

questions.text: The fifth encirclement campaign forced the Communists out of Jiangxi. What made it different from the earlier campaigns?

answers.text: Chiang finally copied the Communists and fought as guerrillas
Japan joined Chiang and attacked the Red Army from the north
Soviet aid to the Communists stopped without warning
Chiang’s armies built lines of small forts and cut off the Communists’ food, so the Red Army could no longer slip away

questions.text: What was the most important result of Zhang Xueliang’s arrest of Chiang at Xi’an in December 1936?

answers.text: It ended Chiang’s plan to crush the Communists first and led to a second united front against Japan
It gave Mao command of the Nationalist army
It made Japan pull its troops out of Manchuria
It kept Chiang a prisoner for the rest of the war

questions.text: By law the army and navy ministers in Japan had to be serving officers. What did this rule allow the military to do?

answers.text: Choose which man would be emperor
Cancel treaties that the Emperor had signed
Bring down any cabinet it disliked by having its minister resign, so civil leaders could never fully control the army
Appoint the members of the parliament

questions.text: The lesson notes that after the Mukden bomb a train passed over the spot soon afterward. Why does the lesson include this detail?

answers.text: It suggests the explosion was too slight to be a real attack, which fits the later finding that Japanese officers set the bomb themselves
It shows that Chinese soldiers were poorly trained in sabotage
It shows that the railway belonged to China and not to Japan
It proves that Tokyo had ordered the attack in advance

questions.text: The Lytton Report judged that Japan’s attack was not self-defense. What does what happened next show?

answers.text: That the commission had not understood the facts
That Japan had proved its case to the League
That Lord Lytton had secretly favored Japan
That a body can judge an aggressor correctly and still have no means to enforce its verdict

questions.text: Mao writes, “the Party commands the gun, and the gun must never be allowed to command the Party.” Why would a student who has just read about Japan notice this sentence?

answers.text: It shows Mao wanted the Communist party to have no army
It names the danger Japan had fallen into, an army that answers to no civil authority, and says his party must prevent it
It shows Mao admired the Kwantung Army and wished to copy it
It shows Mao believed guns have no place in politics

discussions.title: 18.8 Discussion: Was Japan's road to war chosen or forced?
discussions.html:
DISCUSSION
Was Japan’s road to war chosen or forced?
A poor island nation, or an army that stopped taking orders?
Graded discussion · 10 points · one post and one reply
≈ ─ ≈ ─ ≈
HOW TO WORK
Read the two lessons and the two primary sources first, and look over your notes in My Notebook. Then post your answer to the prompt below, and reply to one classmate.
DISCUSSION PROMPT

This week’s question: Was Japan’s road to war chosen or forced?

Choose a side. Give one reason from “Japan: Militarism, Manchuria, and Nanjing” for each side of the question, then say which reason is stronger. Name the step on the road when Japan could most easily have turned back, and say why.

Write 150 to 250 words. State one claim you believe is true. Then explain why, using the specific evidence named above. Keep to what the lessons and the sources show. If you are guessing, say so.

Then add one sentence on perseverance. Does endurance by itself make a cause admirable? Say what you think and why.

RESPOND TO A CLASSMATE

Reply to one classmate. Do you agree with their reasoning? If so, strengthen it with a fact or decision they did not use. If not, say politely where you think it falls short, and give your reason.

GRADING RUBRIC (10 pts)
CriteriaSubstantive (full credit)Thin (partial credit)Missing (no credit)
Your claim and your reasons
6 pts		Takes a clear side, uses the specific evidence the prompt asks for, and explains why it supports the claim.Takes a side but gives general reasons, or leaves out part of what the prompt asks for.No post, or no claim.
Your reply to a classmate
4 pts		Answers one classmate's actual reasoning. Strengthens it or says where it falls short, politely and with a reason.Replies, but only to agree or disagree with no reason.No reply.
10 pts total
